topicTitle: Fungi: General introduction and characteristic features of phycomycetes, ascomycetes, basidiomycetes and deuteromycetes

mcqs.question: The cell wall of fungi is made of:
Penicillium belongs to which fungal group?
The spore-bearing structure of Basidiomycetes is called:
Which of the following is an example of Deuteromycetes?

notes: Fungi: eukaryotic, heterotrophic (absorptive nutrition), cell wall of chitin, no chloroplasts; include moulds, yeasts, mushrooms.

**Deep dive — the absorber's lifestyle.** Fungi cannot ingest; they digest outside their bodies. Hyphae secrete enzymes into the substrate, break large molecules down, and reabsorb the small ones. Combined with chitin cell walls (not cellulose) and a stored carbohydrate of glycogen, this makes the fungus a nutritionally unique kingdom: neither plant (no photosynthesis) nor animal (no ingestion), but the world's premier decomposer and recycling agent.

Four major groups: Phycomycetes (lower fungi, e.g. Rhizopus, water moulds), Ascomycetes (sac fungi, e.g. Penicillium, yeast, morels), Basidiomycetes (club fungi, e.g. Agaricus, rusts, smuts), Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi, no known sexual stage, e.g. Aspergillus, Candida).
Body: mycelium (mass of hyphae); hyphae may be septate (divided) or coenocytic (aseptate).
Reproduction: asexual (spores, budding, fragmentation) and sexual (karyogamy after plasmogamy).
Ascomycetes produce spores in sac-like asci; Basidiomycetes produce spores on basidia (club-shaped bodies).

**Fungal groups — classified by reproduction and hyphae**

| Group | Hyphae | Asexual spores | Sexual spore / structure | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phycomycetes (lower fungi) | Coenocytic (aseptate) | Sporangiospores, zoospores | Zygospore / oospore | Rhizopus (bread mould), Mucor, water moulds |
| Ascomycetes (sac fungi) | Septate | Conidia, budding (yeast) | Ascospores inside asci | Yeast, Penicillium, Aspergillus, morels |
| Basidiomycetes (club fungi) | Septate | Conidia (rare) | Basidiospores on basidia | Mushrooms, rusts, smuts, bracket fungi |
| Deuteromycetes (imperfect) | Septate | Conidia only | Sexual stage unknown | Alternaria, Colletotrichum |
Economic importance: decomposers, food (bread, cheese, mushrooms), medicine (antibiotics — penicillin), industry (enzymes, organic acids); harmful: mycoses, crop blights, aflatoxins.

**Economic importance of fungi — classified ledger**

| Category | Beneficial examples | Harmful examples |
|---|---|---|
| Food industry | Bread and beer (yeast), cheese ripening, mushrooms (Agaricus) | Food spoilage moulds, aflatoxin on grain |
| Medicine | Penicillin (Penicillium), statins, ciclosporin | Ringworm, athlete's foot, aspergillosis |
| Agriculture | Mycorrhizal partners boost uptake; biological control | Rusts, smuts, blights — crop epidemics |
| Industry | Citric acid (Aspergillus), enzymes (amylase, protease) | Rot of timber, textiles, leather |
| Ecology | Decomposers — recycle carbon and nutrients | Some parasitise plants and animals |

```svg Fungal body — mycelium of hyphae
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 380" font-family="Segoe UI" font-size="14"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="380" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="320" y="28" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-weight="bold" fill="#14161a">The fungal body: mycelium = a mat of hyphae</text><line x1="120" y1="140" x2="260" y2="120" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="260" y1="120" x2="390" y2="150" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="390" y1="150" x2="520" y2="130" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="200" y1="200" x2="330" y2="185" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="330" y1="185" x2="480" y2="210" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="150" y1="260" x2="300" y2="250" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="300" y1="250" x2="450" y2="270" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="260" y1="120" x2="330" y2="185" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="390" y1="150" x2="330" y2="185" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="300" y1="250" x2="330" y2="185" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="390" y1="150" x2="450" y2="270" stroke="#7e22ce" stroke-width="3"/><text x="500" y="300" font-size="13" fill="#581c87">hyphae (each a thread)</text><text x="150" y="310" font-size="13" fill="#581c87">mycelium (the whole mat)</text><text x="320" y="345" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#4b5563">Septate hyphae have cross-walls; coenocytic hyphae are one continuous multinucleate tube.</text><text x="320" y="368" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#4b5563">Enzymes pour out of the hyphal tips — digestion happens outside, absorption inside.</text></svg>
```
confusion: Fungi have a chitin cell wall (like arthropods), NOT cellulose (like plants).
Fungi are NOT plants: they are heterotrophic, lack chlorophyll, and are in a separate kingdom.
Deuteromycetes are "imperfect" fungi — they have lost the sexual stage; they are not a true phylogenetic group.
Yeast (Saccharomyces) is an Ascomycete; it reproduces by budding (asexual) but also by forming ascospores.
Rhizopus (bread mould) is a Phycomycete; it reproduces by sporangiospores, not by sexual spores in the lab.
Mushrooms (Agaricus) are Basidiomycetes; the visible mushroom is the fruiting body of the mycelium.

universalFacts: Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, is produced by the fungus Penicillium chrysogenum.
Mycorrhizal fungi form mutualistic associations with ~90% of land plants, aiding phosphorus uptake.
